hld-messaging:0.prompt: What is the core difference in what happens to a message after it is consumed in a RabbitMQ classic queue versus a Kafka topic?
options: Both delete the message once any consumer reads it
RabbitMQ removes it once acked; Kafka keeps it until retention or compaction removes it, whoever has read it
Kafka deletes it once acked; RabbitMQ keeps it for replay
Both keep messages forever unless an admin purges them
hld-messaging:0.explanation: A queue is a work list: once a message is acked it's gone. A log is an append-only record; consumers just move an offset, and data expires by time, size or compaction. That is what makes replay and multiple independent readers cheap in Kafka.

hld-messaging:0.prompt: A bug corrupted a read model built from order events over the last 3 days. You want to fix the code and rebuild from the original events. Which messaging model makes this straightforward?
options: A work queue with competing consumers
A log/stream with sufficient retention, where you reset the consumer offset
Pub/sub over Redis channels
A queue with a dead-letter exchange
hld-messaging:0.explanation: Logs keep events after consumption, so a consumer group can rewind its offsets and reprocess. Queues have already deleted acked messages, and Redis Pub/Sub doesn't persist messages at all.

hld-messaging:0.prompt: Billing, analytics and search each need every 'OrderPlaced' event, and each processes at its own pace. How does a log like Kafka handle this compared with a plain queue?
options: Each service uses its own consumer group with its own offsets, reading the same data once stored
Kafka must copy the topic three times, one per service
All three services must join the same consumer group
Logs cannot support more than one reader per topic
hld-messaging:0.explanation: In a log, consumer groups are independent cursors over shared data. With queues you'd need a fan-out (e.g. a RabbitMQ fanout exchange) that copies each message into one queue per service. Joining one group would split events between the services instead.

hld-messaging:0.prompt: A task system needs per-message priorities, per-message delays and routing by header patterns. Which fits more naturally?
options: Kafka, since partitions can be prioritized
A log with compaction enabled
A traditional broker such as RabbitMQ, with priority queues, TTL/delayed delivery and topic/header exchanges
An S3 bucket polled every minute
hld-messaging:0.explanation: RabbitMQ has priority queues, per-message TTL and routing exchanges built in. Kafka partitions have no priority or per-message delay; you'd emulate them with extra topics. Compaction is about keeping the latest value per key, not scheduling.

hld-messaging:0.prompt: Video transcoding jobs take from 5 seconds to 20 minutes. They run on a Kafka topic with 12 partitions, and short jobs often wait behind long ones. What's the underlying issue?
options: Kafka's retention is too short
Consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count, and each partition is processed in order, so slow jobs block the ones behind them
Kafka cannot store messages larger than 1 KB
The producer is using acks=all
hld-messaging:0.explanation: Kafka assigns each partition to one consumer and processes offsets in order, so a long job causes head-of-line blocking. Queues with competing consumers and per-message acks let any idle worker take the next job, which suits uneven task durations.

hld-messaging:0.prompt: A RabbitMQ queue has 5 competing consumers with prefetch 10. Events for the same account must be processed in order. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, since RabbitMQ delivers in FIFO order so processing stays ordered
Messages for one account can be processed in parallel or out of order across consumers, especially after redelivery
RabbitMQ rejects messages with the same routing key
Prefetch causes messages to be dropped
hld-messaging:0.explanation: Delivery order out of the queue doesn't mean processing order: different consumers finish at different times, and a nacked message is requeued after later ones. Per-key ordering needs partitioning by key, e.g. Kafka keyed partitions or consistent-hash exchanges with one consumer per queue.

hld-messaging:0.prompt: Which statement about Amazon SQS queue types is correct?
options: Standard queues guarantee strict ordering and exactly-once delivery
FIFO queues order messages within a message group and deduplicate within a 5-minute window; standard queues are at-least-once with best-effort ordering
FIFO queues offer unlimited throughput with no ordering
Both types keep messages for up to one year
hld-messaging:0.explanation: SQS Standard offers very high throughput but may deliver duplicates or out of order. FIFO orders per MessageGroupId and deduplicates by deduplication id within 5 minutes. SQS retention is at most 14 days.

hld-messaging:0.prompt: Which are characteristics of a log-based system like Kafka? Select all that apply.
options: Consumers track their own position (offset) in the log
Ordering is guaranteed within a partition
The broker tracks an ack state for every individual message
Data is removed by time/size retention or key-based compaction
hld-messaging:0.explanation: Kafka stores one committed offset per consumer group per partition, not per-message acks. Per-message ack tracking is how queues like RabbitMQ and SQS work. Order is per partition, and retention or compaction controls how long data stays.

hld-messaging:0.prompt: You're adopting event sourcing and want to rebuild new read models from the full history at any time. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: A log with long or infinite retention (or compaction for state topics) supports this
Compaction keeps at least the latest record per key, which suits 'current state' topics
A classic work queue suits this, since consumed messages remain available
SQS alone is unsuitable as the event store because retention maxes out at 14 days
hld-messaging:0.explanation: Rebuilding projections requires stored history, so you need logs with long retention or a durable event store. Compaction keeps the latest value per key for state snapshots. Classic queues delete acked messages, so they can't replay history.

hld-messaging:0.prompt: In Kafka, a slow consumer group holds back other consumer groups reading the same topic.
options: True
False
hld-messaging:0.explanation: Each group has its own offsets, and data stays until retention expires, so a slow group only builds its own lag. The real risk is that a very slow group falls behind retention and loses data that expired before it was read.

hld-messaging:0.prompt: RabbitMQ Streams (introduced in RabbitMQ 3.9) provide an append-only, replayable log in which consumers can start from any offset.
options: True
False
hld-messaging:0.explanation: Streams are a persistent, replicated log type in RabbitMQ. Reading doesn't remove messages, and consumers can attach at first, last, next, an offset or a timestamp. This blurs the old split between queues and logs.

hld-messaging:1.prompt: A topic has 6 partitions. A consumer group scales up to 8 consumers. What happens?
options: Each consumer gets 0.75 partitions on average, so messages are split per record
6 consumers get one partition each and 2 sit idle
Kafka automatically adds 2 partitions to the topic
Every consumer reads all 6 partitions
hld-messaging:1.explanation: Within a group each partition is assigned to at most one consumer, so the partition count caps parallelism. Extra consumers sit idle as hot standbys. Kafka never adds partitions automatically.

hld-messaging:1.prompt: Payment events for each account must be processed in order. How do you achieve this with Kafka?
options: Use a topic with a single partition for the whole system
Set acks=all on the producer
Use the account id as the message key, so the default partitioner sends each account to one partition
Enable log compaction
hld-messaging:1.explanation: Kafka orders records only within a partition. Keying by account id hashes all of an account's events to the same partition, which keeps per-account order and still allows parallelism across accounts. A single partition works but discards all parallelism.

hld-messaging:1.prompt: A keyed topic grows from 12 to 24 partitions. Shortly after, a consumer sees events for one customer out of order. Why?
options: Adding partitions rewrites existing records into new partitions
The key-to-partition mapping changes for new records, so a customer's new events can land on a different partition from their older, unprocessed ones
Consumer offsets reset to earliest when partitions are added
Kafka disables ordering while partitions are being added
hld-messaging:1.explanation: The default partitioner uses hash(key) % numPartitions, so changing the count remaps keys. Old records stay where they were, which allows cross-partition reordering during the transition. That's why keyed topics are sized up front, or migrated to a new topic.

hld-messaging:1.prompt: A topic has replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2, and producers use acks=all. Two of the three replicas go down. What happens to writes?
options: They succeed, acknowledged by the remaining leader
They are buffered by the broker until replicas return
They are written but marked uncommitted
Producers get NotEnoughReplicas errors, since the ISR falls below 2
hld-messaging:1.explanation: acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 requires at least 2 in-sync replicas to accept a write. With only the leader left, Kafka refuses writes instead of risking data loss. This setup tolerates one replica down for writes.

hld-messaging:1.prompt: A Node consumer uses enable.auto.commit=true and hands messages to async workers without waiting. After a crash, some messages were never processed. Why?
options: Auto-commit may commit offsets for messages that were fetched but not yet processed, so they are skipped on restart
Auto-commit always commits offsets in reverse order
Kafka deletes messages once offsets are committed
The broker's retention expired during the crash
hld-messaging:1.explanation: Auto-commit periodically commits the latest polled position, regardless of whether async processing finished. A crash then skips those messages, giving at-most-once behaviour. Commit manually after processing for at-least-once. Committing offsets doesn't delete data.

hld-messaging:1.prompt: A consumer's batch processing sometimes takes 8 minutes. The group keeps rebalancing and messages are reprocessed. Default max.poll.interval.ms is 300000. What's the most direct fix?
options: Increase session.timeout.ms to 10 minutes
Add more partitions
Lower max.poll.records (or raise max.poll.interval.ms) so each poll loop finishes in time
Switch to acks=1
hld-messaging:1.explanation: If poll() isn't called within max.poll.interval.ms, the consumer is considered stuck and evicted, which triggers a rebalance and redelivery. session.timeout.ms covers heartbeats, which run on a background thread, so it doesn't fix slow processing. Smaller batches or a longer interval do.

hld-messaging:1.prompt: What is the trade-off of setting unclean.leader.election.enable=true?
options: Faster rebalances but more duplicates on the consumer side
A partition can stay available by electing an out-of-sync replica, at the cost of losing committed messages
Stronger durability at the cost of higher producer latency
It allows two leaders per partition for higher throughput
hld-messaging:1.explanation: If every in-sync replica is gone, unclean election lets a lagging replica become leader. Writes resume, but messages it never received are lost. The default (false) keeps the partition offline instead, choosing consistency over availability.

hld-messaging:1.prompt: Ops reports 'consumer lag = 2,000,000' for the analytics group on partition 3. What does this number mean?
options: 2 million messages failed processing
The partition's log-end offset is 2 million ahead of the group's committed offset
The consumer is 2 million milliseconds behind wall clock
The partition holds 2 million messages in total
hld-messaging:1.explanation: Lag is log-end offset minus committed offset: how many records the group hasn't yet confirmed processing. Lag measured as time is a separate metric that some tools derive. Lag says nothing about failures by itself.

hld-messaging:1.prompt: Which statements about Kafka replication are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A follower drops out of the ISR if it doesn't catch up within replica.lag.time.max.ms
Consumers read only up to the high watermark, the offset replicated to all in-sync replicas
By default, a new leader is elected only from the ISR
With acks=1 the producer waits for every ISR member to acknowledge
hld-messaging:1.explanation: With acks=1 only the leader acknowledges, so data can be lost if the leader fails before followers copy it. acks=all waits for the full ISR. The high watermark stops consumers seeing records that could disappear on failover.

hld-messaging:1.prompt: Which statements about Kafka log compaction are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It retains at least the latest record for each key
A record with a null value (tombstone) eventually removes the key, after delete.retention.ms
Offsets of surviving records are unchanged; compaction does not renumber them
It guarantees consumers never see an older value for any key
hld-messaging:1.explanation: Compaction runs in the background on closed segments, so the uncompacted head can still hold several values per key, and a consumer may see old ones. It keeps the latest value per key, keeps original offsets (leaving gaps), and tombstones delete keys.

hld-messaging:1.prompt: By default, Kafka consumer groups store committed offsets in the internal __consumer_offsets topic, not in ZooKeeper.
options: True
False
hld-messaging:1.explanation: Since Kafka 0.9, offsets have been committed to the compacted __consumer_offsets topic, managed by the group coordinator. ZooKeeper-based offsets are legacy, and Kafka 4.x drops ZooKeeper entirely in favour of KRaft.

hld-messaging:2.prompt: A consumer acks each message as soon as it's received, then processes it. If it crashes mid-processing, which delivery semantics results?
options: At-least-once
Exactly-once
At-most-once
Effectively-once
hld-messaging:2.explanation: Acking first means the broker won't redeliver, so a crash loses the message: at most once. Acking after processing gives at-least-once, since a crash before the ack causes redelivery and possible duplicates.

hld-messaging:2.prompt: A worker sends a welcome email and then acks the message. Sometimes users get two emails. What is the most likely cause?
options: The broker is configured for at-most-once delivery
The worker crashed or the ack was lost after sending, so the message was redelivered under at-least-once semantics
The email provider is replaying old requests
Two different queues hold the same message by design
hld-messaging:2.explanation: Process-then-ack is at-least-once: if the ack never reaches the broker, the message comes back. The fix is idempotency, e.g. record 'welcome sent for user X' or pass an idempotency key to the email provider.

hld-messaging:2.prompt: An SQS consumer takes about 90 seconds per message. The queue's visibility timeout is 30 seconds. What happens?
options: SQS waits for the consumer to finish before redelivering
The message becomes visible again after 30 seconds and another consumer processes it concurrently
The message is moved straight to the DLQ
SQS rejects messages that take longer than the timeout
hld-messaging:2.explanation: After the visibility timeout, SQS assumes the consumer failed and makes the message visible again, which causes duplicate processing. Set the timeout above the processing time or extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility as a heartbeat.

hld-messaging:2.prompt: You dedupe at-least-once deliveries by message id. What is the most robust way to store 'already processed' markers when the side effect is a Postgres write?
options: An in-memory Set inside each consumer process
A Redis key written after the Postgres transaction commits
A processed_messages row with a unique message_id, inserted in the same Postgres transaction as the side effect
A log line that you grep on redelivery
hld-messaging:2.explanation: Writing the marker atomically with the effect means both happen or neither does; a unique constraint also catches concurrent duplicates. Writing Redis after commit leaves a gap where a crash leaves the effect done but unmarked. In-memory sets vanish on restart.

hld-messaging:2.prompt: A Kafka Streams-style app uses transactions to consume, transform and produce. Which downstream consumer setting is required so it doesn't see records from aborted transactions?
options: isolation.level=read_committed
enable.auto.commit=false
auto.offset.reset=earliest
acks=all
hld-messaging:2.explanation: The default isolation.level=read_uncommitted returns records from aborted transactions too. read_committed reads only up to the last stable offset and filters aborted data. acks is a producer setting.

hld-messaging:2.prompt: A Node service publishes to RabbitMQ without publisher confirms, on persistent messages to a durable queue. The broker restarts. What can happen?
options: Nothing is lost, because durable queues and persistent messages are enough
Messages the publisher thinks it sent can be lost if they weren't yet written to disk; confirms let you retry them
All messages are delivered twice after restart
The broker converts the queue to transient
hld-messaging:2.explanation: Without confirms the publisher never learns whether the broker safely stored a message. Confirms (plus retrying unconfirmed messages) give at-least-once publishing, at the cost of possible duplicates, which consumers then deduplicate.

hld-messaging:2.prompt: What does Kafka's idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true, the default since Kafka 3.0) prevent?
options: Consumers processing the same record twice
Duplicate records in a partition caused by producer retries, detected using a producer id and sequence numbers
Messages being lost when a broker disk fails
Two applications sending identical payloads
hld-messaging:2.explanation: The broker tracks (producer id, partition, sequence) and drops retried batches it has already written. It protects only that producer session's writes; it doesn't stop consumer-side redelivery or deduplicate across different producers.

hld-messaging:2.prompt: In an at-least-once system, which situations lead to duplicate processing? Select all that apply.
options: The consumer crashes after the side effect but before acking
The ack is lost on the network, so the broker redelivers
The producer retries after a timeout although the broker had already stored the message
The consumer acks before starting to process
hld-messaging:2.explanation: Duplicates come from uncertainty: a lost ack or a lost produce response leads to a retry. Acking before processing causes message loss rather than duplicates; that's at-most-once.

hld-messaging:2.prompt: A consumer charges customer cards from Kafka events. Which measures give effectively-once charging? Select all that apply.
options: Send a deterministic idempotency key (e.g. the event id) with each payment provider call
Record processed event ids in a table with a unique constraint
Rely on Kafka transactions alone, since they cover external API calls
Increase producer retries so delivery becomes exactly-once
hld-messaging:2.explanation: External side effects need their own deduplication: idempotency keys stop the provider charging twice, and a unique-keyed record lets you skip redeliveries. Kafka transactions only cover Kafka reads and writes, and more retries add duplicates rather than removing them.

hld-messaging:2.prompt: Kafka Streams can provide exactly-once processing for Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2.
options: True
False
hld-messaging:2.explanation: exactly_once_v2 uses transactions to atomically commit output records, state-store changelogs and input offsets. It covers effects within Kafka, while calls to external systems from inside the topology still need idempotency.

hld-messaging:2.prompt: At-most-once delivery is never an acceptable choice for a production system.
options: True
False
hld-messaging:2.explanation: For high-volume, low-value data such as metrics samples, telemetry or presence pings, losing an occasional message is fine and avoids the cost of retries and deduplication. The right choice depends on what a lost message costs.

hld-messaging:3.prompt: A message with malformed JSON fails every time it's consumed and is retried forever, blocking the queue. What's the standard remedy?
options: Increase the consumer's memory
After a bounded number of attempts, move it to a dead-letter queue for inspection
Delete the whole queue and recreate it
Lower the prefetch count to 1
hld-messaging:3.explanation: A poison message will never succeed, so endless retries waste capacity and can block messages behind it. A DLQ isolates it while keeping it for debugging and possible redrive. Prefetch changes throughput but not this failure.

hld-messaging:3.prompt: A downstream API has a 30-second outage. 10,000 clients all retry with pure exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s...) and no jitter. What problem appears when the API recovers?
options: Retries are spread evenly over time
Clients retry in synchronized waves that hit the recovering service at the same moments
Exponential backoff stops retrying after 30 seconds
Clients give up immediately
hld-messaging:3.explanation: Clients that failed together keep retrying together, causing thundering-herd spikes that can knock the service over again. Jitter randomizes each delay to spread the load. Plain backoff stretches out the gaps, but clients stay in lockstep.

hld-messaging:3.prompt: Retries use exponential backoff: retry n waits 1s × 2^(n−1), with no jitter. What is the total waiting time across 5 retries?
options: 16 seconds
31 seconds
32 seconds
63 seconds
hld-messaging:3.explanation: Delays are 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 seconds. 16 is only the last delay, and 63 would be the total for 6 retries. Estimates like this help size visibility timeouts and alert thresholds.

hld-messaging:3.prompt: A consumer calls a partner API. Which failure should go straight to the DLQ without retries?
options: 503 Service Unavailable
A connection timeout
400 Bad Request caused by an invalid field in the message
429 Too Many Requests
hld-messaging:3.explanation: A 400 caused by the message's content will fail the same way every time, so retrying only adds load and delay. 503, timeouts and 429 are usually transient and worth retrying with backoff (respecting Retry-After for 429).

hld-messaging:3.prompt: A Kafka consumer retries failed messages in place with sleeps of up to 10 minutes. Lag explodes on that partition. What's a common pattern to avoid this, and its main cost?
options: Increase partitions; the cost is higher broker CPU
Republish failures to delayed retry topics (e.g. retry-1m, retry-10m) and then a DLT; the cost is losing strict per-key ordering
Use acks=0; the cost is message loss
Disable retries entirely; the cost is nothing
hld-messaging:3.explanation: Blocking retries stall everything behind the failing record in that partition. Non-blocking retry topics keep the main partition moving, but a failed record is then processed after later records with the same key, so ordering-sensitive flows need extra care.

hld-messaging:3.prompt: A bug sent 50,000 messages to the DLQ. You've deployed a fix and want to redrive them. Which concern is most important?
options: DLQ messages must be re-encrypted before redrive
Make sure consumers are idempotent and throttle the redrive, since some messages may have been partly processed and a burst can overload dependencies
Redrive in reverse order to restore causality
Redriven messages always lose their payload
hld-messaging:3.explanation: Some messages may have had partial side effects before failing, so replay must be safe to repeat; dumping 50k at once can also swamp downstream services. Also watch for stale messages that newer events have superseded. Reversing order doesn't restore causality.

hld-messaging:3.prompt: In Amazon SQS, what decides when a failing message moves to the dead-letter queue?
options: The message's retention period
The redrive policy's maxReceiveCount: after that many receives without deletion, SQS moves it
The consumer must explicitly call a SendToDLQ API
The visibility timeout reaching zero once
hld-messaging:3.explanation: SQS counts receives. When ApproximateReceiveCount exceeds maxReceiveCount, the message goes to the configured DLQ. Each failed attempt is one receive whose visibility timeout expires without a delete.

hld-messaging:3.prompt: When dead-lettering a message, what context is worth attaching so on-call engineers can debug and redrive it? Select all that apply.
options: The original payload, unchanged
The last error message or stack trace
The attempt count and first/last failure timestamps
The source topic/queue (and partition/offset if relevant)
Only the message id, to save space
hld-messaging:3.explanation: Debugging and redriving require the exact payload, why it failed, how often, and where it came from. Storing only an id forces you to reconstruct the message, which may be impossible once the source has expired it.

hld-messaging:3.prompt: Which retry practices help protect a struggling downstream service? Select all that apply.
options: Full jitter: sleep a random time between 0 and min(cap, base × 2^attempt)
Cap the maximum delay and the number of attempts
Use a retry budget or circuit breaker to stop retries from amplifying an outage
Retry immediately in a tight loop to minimize latency
hld-messaging:3.explanation: Jitter spreads load, caps bound the worst case, and budgets or circuit breakers stop retry storms multiplying traffic during an incident. Tight-loop retries are the classic way to turn a partial outage into a full one.

hld-messaging:3.prompt: DLQ depth should be monitored and alerted on, because a growing DLQ usually means a bug or a downstream outage.
options: True
False
hld-messaging:3.explanation: A DLQ nobody watches is where data quietly disappears. Alerting on depth or arrival rate surfaces deploy regressions, schema changes and partner outages quickly, before retention deletes the messages.

hld-messaging:3.prompt: Retrying a non-idempotent operation is safe as long as you wait long enough between attempts.
options: True
False
hld-messaging:3.explanation: Backoff controls load, not correctness. If the first attempt actually succeeded but its response was lost, any retry repeats the side effect. Non-idempotent operations need idempotency keys or deduplication before retrying them.

hld-messaging:4.prompt: A service commits an order to Postgres and then publishes 'OrderCreated' to Kafka. What happens if the process crashes between the two steps?
options: Postgres rolls back the order automatically
The order exists but the event is never published, so downstream services never learn about it
Kafka publishes the event from its write-ahead log
The event is published twice
hld-messaging:4.explanation: This is the dual-write problem: two systems with no shared transaction. Committing then crashing loses the event; publishing first then failing the commit creates a phantom event. The transactional outbox solves this by writing the event in the same DB transaction.

hld-messaging:4.prompt: How does the transactional outbox pattern ensure an event is published if and only if the business change commits?
options: It wraps the DB write and the Kafka publish in a 2PC transaction
It inserts the event into an outbox table in the same DB transaction as the change; a separate relay publishes it later
It publishes to Kafka first and has consumers write to the DB
It retries the Kafka publish inside the DB transaction until it succeeds
hld-messaging:4.explanation: The outbox row commits or rolls back atomically with the business data. A relay (poller or CDC) then publishes committed rows at least once. No distributed transaction is needed, and nothing slow runs inside the DB transaction.

hld-messaging:4.prompt: Compared with a relay that polls the outbox table every second, what does log-based CDC (e.g. Debezium reading the PostgreSQL WAL) mainly offer?
options: Exactly-once delivery to consumers
Lower latency and no polling queries on the DB, at the cost of running CDC infrastructure and needing logical replication
No need for the outbox table at all in any design
Strict global ordering across all tables
hld-messaging:4.explanation: CDC streams committed changes from the transaction log in near real time, without SELECT polling load. It needs wal_level=logical, a replication slot and a connector to operate. Delivery is still at-least-once, so consumers must deduplicate.

hld-messaging:4.prompt: An outbox relay publishes a row, crashes before marking it as sent, restarts and publishes it again. How should the system cope?
options: Use 2PC between the relay and Kafka
Consumers deduplicate using a unique event id carried in each outbox message
Delete outbox rows before publishing them
Run only one consumer instance
hld-messaging:4.explanation: Outbox relays are inherently at-least-once, since 'publish' and 'mark sent' can't be atomic. Each event has a stable id so consumers can detect repeats. Deleting before publishing turns this into possible event loss.

hld-messaging:4.prompt: Debezium was down for two days over a weekend. On Monday the PostgreSQL primary's disk is nearly full. What is the most likely cause?
options: The outbox table has no index
The logical replication slot kept WAL that the absent consumer hadn't confirmed, so WAL piled up
Autovacuum is disabled on the outbox table
Debezium writes snapshots to the primary's disk
hld-messaging:4.explanation: A replication slot makes PostgreSQL keep WAL until the consumer confirms it, so a stalled consumer causes unbounded WAL growth. Monitor slot lag and set max_slot_wal_keep_size (PostgreSQL 13+) to cap it. An outbox table without vacuum bloats too, but far more slowly than retained WAL.

hld-messaging:4.prompt: To scale a polling outbox relay you run 3 instances, each running SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100. What problem can this introduce?
options: Deadlocks on every poll
Events for the same aggregate can be published out of order, since different instances take different rows
SKIP LOCKED makes rows invisible permanently
Postgres rejects concurrent FOR UPDATE queries
hld-messaging:4.explanation: SKIP LOCKED spreads rows across workers without blocking, but two events for the same order may be published by different instances in either order. Partition work by aggregate id or use a single active relay (leader election) when per-aggregate order matters.

hld-messaging:4.prompt: Why not publish the event to Kafka inside the DB transaction, before COMMIT, to avoid the dual-write problem?
options: Kafka rejects messages sent during an open DB transaction
If the transaction later rolls back, the event is already out: a phantom event for a change that never happened
It reduces Kafka throughput by half
Postgres forbids network calls inside transactions
hld-messaging:4.explanation: Publishing before commit just reverses the failure: consumers may act on an order that rolled back. It also holds DB locks during a network call. Postgres doesn't forbid the call, but nothing ties its result to the commit.

hld-messaging:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL, an outbox relay polls with the query below and remembers the highest id it has published. Occasionally an event is never published. Why?
hld-messaging:4.code:
SELECT * FROM outbox
WHERE id > $1   -- last published id
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 100;
options: ORDER BY id is non-deterministic for bigserial columns
LIMIT skips rows when there are more than 100
Sequence values are assigned before commit, so a transaction holding a lower id can commit after the relay has moved past it
PostgreSQL reuses deleted ids
hld-messaging:4.explanation: Transaction A gets id 10, B gets 11; B commits first, the relay publishes 11 and moves its cursor past 10. When A commits, id 10 is never seen. Use a 'published' flag, or CDC, which reads in commit order. LIMIT just pages; the next poll continues.

hld-messaging:4.prompt: Which columns are useful in an outbox table? Select all that apply.
options: A unique event id
Aggregate type and aggregate id (useful for routing and partition keys)
The serialized event payload
Created-at timestamp
The downstream consumer group's committed offset
hld-messaging:4.explanation: The event id enables deduplication, aggregate fields drive topic routing and keys (which keep per-aggregate order), and the payload and timestamp describe the event. Consumer offsets belong to the broker or consumer, not the producer's outbox.

hld-messaging:4.prompt: Comparing CDC directly on business tables with CDC on a dedicated outbox table, which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Direct table CDC turns your internal schema into a public contract for consumers
An outbox lets you publish explicit, versioned domain events shaped for consumers
Both avoid the dual-write problem, since events come from committed DB changes
Direct table CDC naturally captures business intent such as 'OrderShipped' vs 'AddressCorrected'
hld-messaging:4.explanation: Row-level CDC emits 'row changed' facts tied to your schema, so renaming a column breaks consumers, and intent is lost: an update to status looks the same whatever the reason. Outbox events are designed contracts. Both read committed data, so both avoid dual writes.

hld-messaging:4.prompt: Debezium's Outbox Event Router transformation can route outbox rows to Kafka topics based on an aggregate type column.
options: True
False
hld-messaging:4.explanation: The Outbox Event Router SMT reads outbox inserts, routes by the aggregatetype field (configurable) to topics like outbox.event.<type>, uses the aggregate id as the message key, and passes the payload through as the message value.

hld-messaging:5.prompt: What does 'back-pressure' mean in a data pipeline?
options: Retrying failed messages with increasing delays
A slower downstream stage signalling upstream to slow down or stop sending, so buffers stay bounded
Compressing messages to reduce network usage
Sending acknowledgements back to producers
hld-messaging:5.explanation: Back-pressure is flow control: demand flows upstream so producers never outrun consumers without limit. Retries with backoff are a different mechanism, although both involve slowing down.

hld-messaging:5.prompt: In Node.js, writable.write(chunk) returns false. What should well-behaved code do?
options: Throw an error because the write failed
Retry the same chunk immediately
Stop writing and resume after the stream emits 'drain'
Call writable.end() and open a new stream
hld-messaging:5.explanation: false means the internal buffer has reached highWaterMark; the chunk was still accepted. Keep writing anyway and memory grows without limit. Wait for 'drain', or use pipeline(), which handles this for you.

hld-messaging:5.prompt: An ingestion service pushes incoming webhooks into an in-memory array that workers drain. During a traffic spike, the pod gets OOM-killed. What's the best structural fix?
options: Give the pod more memory
Use a bounded queue: when full, slow intake (e.g. respond 429/503) or persist to a durable broker
Process items in LIFO order
Use a Map instead of an array
hld-messaging:5.explanation: An unbounded buffer only delays failure. A bounded buffer forces a decision when full: push back, shed load, or move to durable storage such as a broker. More memory buys time but doesn't change the failure mode.

hld-messaging:5.prompt: Why do pull-based consumers, as in Kafka, provide natural back-pressure compared with brokers that push without limits?
options: Pull consumers fetch only when ready, so a slow consumer builds lag in the durable log instead of piling up messages in its memory
Pull is always faster than push
Brokers that push cannot persist messages
Pull consumers never need to commit offsets
hld-messaging:5.explanation: With pull, the consumer sets the pace and the excess stays in the broker's storage as lag. Push systems need explicit limits (e.g. RabbitMQ prefetch) or they can flood consumers. Pull isn't inherently faster.

hld-messaging:5.prompt: An API's p99 latency climbs to 30 s under overload, and most requests time out on the client anyway. What's the better server-side strategy?
options: Accept every request and add more worker threads
Reject excess requests early with 503/429 when queue depth or queueing time exceeds a threshold, prioritizing critical traffic
Increase client timeouts to 60 seconds
Queue requests on disk and answer them hours later
hld-messaging:5.explanation: Work for requests whose clients have already given up is wasted and delays everyone else. Load shedding keeps latency bounded for accepted requests. Longer timeouts only lengthen the queue, and unbounded workers add contention.

hld-messaging:5.prompt: This script copies a 20 GB file and its memory use climbs to several GB. Why?
options: createReadStream loads the whole file before emitting 'data'
Disk writes are slower than reads and write()'s false return value is ignored, so chunks pile up in dst's buffer
The 'end' handler runs before any data is written
fs streams default to a 1 GB highWaterMark
hld-messaging:5.explanation: The reader keeps emitting while the writer's buffer grows, since nobody pauses src when write() returns false. Use pipeline(src, dst) or src.pipe(dst), which pause and resume on 'drain'. The default highWaterMark is 64 KiB for fs read streams.

hld-messaging:5.prompt: A job calls await Promise.all(userIds.map(id => fetchProfile(id))) with 1,000,000 ids against a partner API. What's the main problem?
options: Promise.all runs the requests one after another, which is slow
All requests start at once: unbounded concurrency exhausts sockets and memory and floods the partner
Promise.all cannot handle more than 65,536 promises
fetchProfile results come back in random order
hld-messaging:5.explanation: map() starts every call immediately; Promise.all only waits for them. Use bounded concurrency (a worker pool, p-limit, or batching) so in-flight requests stay capped. Promise.all preserves result order and has no 65,536 limit.

hld-messaging:5.prompt: Which are legitimate strategies when a producer outpaces a consumer? Select all that apply.
options: Buffer in a bounded queue
Drop or sample excess data where loss is acceptable
Block or pause the producer until there's capacity
Rate-limit the producer
Grow the in-memory buffer without limit
hld-messaging:5.explanation: The classic options are buffer (bounded), drop, block, or control the producer's rate. An unbounded buffer just postpones the problem until the process runs out of memory, so it isn't a strategy.

hld-messaging:5.prompt: A Node.js Kafka consumer calls a slow downstream API for each message. Which techniques apply back-pressure correctly? Select all that apply.
options: Pause partitions when in-flight work exceeds a limit, and resume as it drains
Cap the number of concurrent in-flight messages per partition or per consumer
Scale consumers up to the partition count to add throughput
Fetch as fast as possible into an in-memory array and process it later
hld-messaging:5.explanation: Pausing fetches and bounding concurrency keep memory flat and let lag build in Kafka, where it's durable. Adding consumers up to the partition count increases throughput. Draining the broker into RAM removes the back-pressure that pull-based consumption provides.

hld-messaging:5.prompt: Node's stream.pipeline() handles back-pressure between stages and also forwards errors and cleans up every stream in the chain.
options: True
False
hld-messaging:5.explanation: pipeline() (or its promise form in stream/promises) wires up back-pressure like pipe(), and also destroys every stream and reports the error if any stage fails. Plain .pipe() doesn't forward errors, so streams can leak.

hld-messaging:5.prompt: TCP has no built-in back-pressure, so applications must implement all flow control themselves.
options: True
False
hld-messaging:5.explanation: TCP's receive window is flow control: a slow receiver shrinks the window and the sender's writes eventually block or buffer. Node surfaces this as socket.write() returning false. Applications still need back-pressure at higher levels, such as queues and worker pools.
